title: The First 5 Hires: Recruiting Roadmap for Seed Startups (August 2026)
summary: October 2026 recruiting roadmap for seed startups: how to sequence your first 5 hires and when to bring in a recruiter.
body_markdown:
Everyone agrees early hires matter, but far fewer founders get a clear[recruiting roadmap](https://www.dover.com/) for who to hire first and why. At the seed stage, each teammate helps shape how decisions get made, how fast you move, and what habits take root as you grow. This guide explains how to sequence your first five hires around the skills your founding team lacks and the milestones ahead. The right order depends on your product, sales process, and current team.


**TLDR:**


-


Your first five hires help set working habits that can last as the team grows; their share of headcount depends on the number of founders and other employees.


-


Hire a founding engineer first if you’re building tech; they ship fast and own decisions with minimal direction.


-


Choose sales over marketing for deals above $50K; marketing first for sub-$10K self-service products.


-


A free ATS can help with candidate tracking and job distribution, but included features vary by provider. Check the plan comparison for free and paid feature limits.


-


Some tools pair a free ATS with paid fractional recruiting support. Recruiter pricing options can include hourly, retainer, and pay-per-hire agreements; the best fit depends on workload and budget.


## How Your First 5 Hires Can Shape Your Startup’s Success


Your first five hires will touch many parts of your startup. They may write the code that defines your product architecture, close early deals, and set the tone for how your team works together. At the seed stage, a small team gives each person considerable influence. Their decisions, work habits, and interactions can create patterns that persist as you scale.


## Identifying Your Critical Skill Gaps before You Start Hiring


Start by mapping what you need to hit your next milestone against what your founding team can actually do. If you need to ship a working product in three months and neither founder can code, you have an obvious gap. If you’ve built the product but have no customers, you need someone who can sell.


Look for bottlenecks too.


## The Founding Engineer: Building Your Technical Foundation


If you’re building a tech product,[hiring top engineers](https://www.dover.com/blog/how-to-hire-engineers-your-ultimate-guide) can be a sensible first move unless you have a technical co-founder who can code full-time. If you’re building any kind of tech product, this should be your first hire unless you have a technical co-founder who can code full-time.


But a founding engineer is different from engineer number ten. You’re not looking for someone who executes tickets and follows existing patterns. You need someone who can make architectural decisions with incomplete information, ship features in days instead of weeks, and own entire product surfaces without guidance.


The best founding engineers optimize for learning speed over code perfection.


Look for past experience at the zero-to-one stage.


Your founding engineer should be excited about finding product-market fit. If they only want to focus on technical problems and never talk to customers, they’re wrong for this stage.


## Sales vs. Marketing: Which Revenue Function Comes First


The answer starts with your deal size and sales cycle. If you’re selling contracts worth $50,000+ that require multiple demos, negotiation, and executive sign-off, you need a salesperson first. Someone has to own the full sales cycle, build relationships, and close deals. Marketing content won’t move these buyers without human interaction.


If your product costs less than $10,000 and buyers can sign up with a credit card, marketing comes first. You need inbound leads, content that drives organic traffic, and a funnel that converts visitors into trial users. A salesperson calling small-ticket buyers who expect self-service will feel out of place.


One more factor: founder skill set. If you can sell but can’t write or run ads, hire marketing. If you’re good at content but terrible at closing deals, hire sales. Your first go-to-market hire should fill the gap you can’t cover yourself while you focus on product and fundraising.


## Setting Up Your Hiring Infrastructure from Day One


Most founders wait until they’re scheduling interviews to think about process. By then, you’re already behind. Building basic hiring infrastructure before you need it can help you move faster when you find good candidates instead of scrambling to figure out next steps.


Start with a[simple applicant tracking system](https://www.dover.com/ats) . You need somewhere to collect applications, store resumes, and track where each candidate stands. Spreadsheets work until you’re juggling ten active candidates across three roles. Then you lose track of who you emailed back, who’s waiting on feedback, and which resume belonged to the person you actually liked.


Your interview process should be defined before you post the job. Decide upfront how many interview rounds you’ll run, who needs to meet each candidate, and what you’re assessing at each stage. One common early-stage process includes a screening call, a technical or functional evaluation, and a team fit conversation. Write down the questions you’ll ask. This keeps you consistent across candidates so you can actually compare them fairly.


## The Role of a Free ATS in Managing Your First 5 Hires


A[free ATS](https://www.dover.com/blog/startup-ats-guide) can reduce coordination problems during early hiring by keeping candidate status in one place. When you’re managing five candidates for your first engineering role, email threads and spreadsheets feel manageable. When you’re hiring for three roles at once and each has ten candidates at different stages, you need a single place to see who’s waiting on feedback, who needs to be scheduled, and who went cold.


The features that matter most are simple. A customizable interview plan shows which stage each candidate is in, notes with @mentions keep feedback attached to the candidate profile, and job-board posting from one screen saves you from re-entering the same role. Many free plans include these, though limits on items like feedback forms vary by provider.


## When to Bring in External Recruiting Support


You’re ready for[external recruiting help](https://www.dover.com/blog/signs-startup-hire-recruiter) when hiring starts blocking your ability to run the company. If you’re spending 15+ hours per week sourcing candidates, screening resumes, and scheduling interviews instead of talking to customers or building product, you need support.


Specialized roles are another clear signal. Finding engineers with experience in your specific tech stack, or sales leaders who’ve sold into your target market, requires networks you probably don’t have. A[fractional recruiter](https://www.dover.com/recruiters) who’s placed 50 machine learning engineers knows where to find number 51. You don’t.


Fractional recruiters can suit seed-stage teams that need recruiting help without a full-time salary commitment.[KORE1’s 2026 tech recruiter salary guide](https://www.kore1.com/tech-recruiter-salary-guide/) reports a broad range of in-house base pay, with compensation varying by experience and market. Benefits, payroll taxes, and other costs add to the hiring budget. On an[hourly fractional engagement](https://www.dover.com/blog/fractional-recruiter-costs) , you pay for time worked; Dover’s recruiter marketplace also supports retainer and pay-per-hire agreements. Scope, budget, and the ability to reduce hours depend on the arrangement you choose.


An ATS and a fractional recruiter solve different problems. The ATS handles coordination: applications, candidate stages, and feedback in one place. A fractional recruiter adds sourcing capacity for specialized roles or when you have no time to reach candidates who aren’t applying. Putting the ATS in place first lets the recruiter work inside the same pipeline from day one. Both sides can then see who has been contacted, which can help prevent duplicate outreach.


## The Seed-Stage Hiring Market in October 2026


Venture funding remains uneven across companies and sectors.[Crunchbase’s Q3 2026 funding report](https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/q3-2026-global-startup-funding-ai-billion-dollar-rounds-exits-data/) , based on data as of October 2, shows global investment falling from the prior quarter while remaining above the year-earlier level. Large rounds and AI companies account for much of that capital. These funding totals do not measure seed-stage hiring demand, so they are useful context, not evidence that every startup faces the same competition for candidates.


A few distinctions can help founders interpret the market without treating broad trends as hiring rules:


-


**AI funding is concentrated, but offer counts are unverified.** Crunchbase’s Q3 report shows AI companies received most venture funding, not how many offers engineers receive. Role-specific candidate feedback guides an offer better than an assumed market-wide count.


-


**Recruiter involvement may vary by team size.** Ashby’s 2026 startup hiring report suggests that recruiter involvement increases with company size. Its findings do not show that fractional recruiting is the default for seed-stage startups. Founder-led, fractional, and full-time recruiting remain different choices for different workloads.


-


**Funding headlines are not a hiring budget.** Large seed rounds skew the totals, so build your hiring plan around your own runway and next milestone, not other startups’ fundraising.


-


**Recruiter involvement may be associated with shorter hiring timelines at smaller startups.** Ashby’s 2026 data suggests this link, but it does not prove a recruiter will shorten every search.


## Building Dover into Your Seed Stage Recruiting Roadmap


Early-stage hiring has two layers. The first is coordination: collecting applications, tracking candidate status, sharing feedback, and distributing your job to boards. An ATS covers this well. The second is sourcing capacity: reaching candidates who aren’t actively applying anywhere. Software alone doesn’t fill that gap; fractional recruiters can.


Setting up a free ATS before you start sourcing also keeps sourcing notes, outreach history, and candidate data in your own pipeline instead of with an outside recruiter. Later searches can then build on earlier ones instead of starting from zero.


Dover’s free plan lists unlimited jobs, users, and candidate tracking, plus a basic careers page, job-board distribution, resume search, and a Chrome sourcing extension. Candidate profile history and analytics history are limited on Free. AI applicant scoring and the AI notetaker come with the $199/month Premium plan, which also adds bulk actions, advanced scheduling, and data export. Scoring can support resume review against your criteria, but hiring teams still make the decisions.


For roles that need specialized sourcing, Dover pairs its ATS with a marketplace of fractional recruiters who can work in Dover’s ATS or your existing tools. Published founder reviews can help you assess a recruiter’s past work. Hourly is the primary pricing model, with recruiter-set rates and a budget agreed before work begins; retainer and pay-per-hire agreements are also available, and no long-term contract is required. ## FAQs


### What hiring tools do Y Combinator startups actually use?


Public examples include YC’s Work at a Startup job board and Dover’s recruiting tools.[YC’s jobs page](https://www.ycombinator.com/jobs) is a channel for reaching candidates interested in YC companies. Dover’s YC company profile describes a free ATS and access to fractional recruiters. These sources show available tools, not a survey of which ATS most YC startups choose. The useful distinction is where candidates find jobs versus where your team tracks applications, and one tool does not have to cover both.


### What makes a founding engineer different from a regular engineer hire?


A founding engineer makes architectural decisions with incomplete information, can ship small features quickly when scope allows, and owns entire product surfaces without guidance. They optimize for learning speed over code perfection and are comfortable throwing away work based on customer feedback.


### Do I need a recruiter if I’m already using an ATS?


An ATS handles coordination: collecting applications, tracking candidate stages, and distributing your job to boards. A fractional recruiter adds sourcing depth for roles where inbound alone won’t fill the gap. If inbound volume is sufficient, an ATS covers what you need. If the role is specialized, senior, or you have no bandwidth to source, a fractional recruiter works on top of the ATS as an added capacity layer. They solve different parts of the same problem.


## Final Thoughts on Getting Early Hiring Right


Getting early hiring right comes down to clarity, speed, and having a[recruiting roadmap](https://www.dover.com/) that matches the reality of the seed stage. Founders need a clear view of where they fall short and a fast way to bring in people who can operate in ambiguity and build from zero to one. With limited runway, hiring mistakes can compound, so the right foundation often counts for more than the right pace. Software can keep the process organized, and a fractional recruiter can add sourcing capacity when a search outgrows what a founder can cover alone. Dover is one example of that framework: a free ATS paired with on-demand fractional recruiters in one shared system, with no long-term contract required.
